text: Executive Summary

SRK Consulting (Canada), Inc. (SRK) and Paterson and Cooke (P&C), referred herein as SRK-PC, were appointed by Canada Nickel Co. (CN) to undertake the site-specific seismic hazard assessment for the Crawford Project site near Timmins, Ontario as part of the activities to support of the Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) for the proposed facilities. A Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Assessment (PSHA) was carried out for representative site conditions at the Crawford site. Design ground motions and guidance for the embankments are provided in terms of peak ground acceleration, spectral accelerations, and horizontal seismic coefficients for stability analysis.

The Crawford Project site is located within the stable craton of the North American plate, in Northern Ontario region, characterized by a recently deglaciated shield terrain with numerous lakes, crystalline bedrock exposures, and variable glacial till deposits (Chapter 0). While Northern Ontario has a low rate of seismicity, notable intraplate seismicity has been recorded, driven primarily by Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) and regional intraplate stress. These forces, along with the reactivation of crustal faults and fractures, contribute to the region's earthquake activity.

The seismicity analysis for the Crawford Project site (Chapter 0) is based on data from publicly available databases, which were utilized to update the seismic catalog within a 400-kilometer radius of the site. The updated and declustered catalog documents 67 events with moment magnitudes (Mw) of 3 or greater, spanning from 1916 to August 30, 2026. Historical events such as the 1935 Temiskamingue earthquake (Mw 6.2) and the 2000 Kipawa earthquake (Mw 4.7) demonstrate the potential for notable seismic activity.

The seismic hazard assessment for the Crawford Project site (Chapter 0) utilized the 6th Generation Seismic Hazard Model of Canada (CanadaSHM6) (Canadian Comission on Building and Fires Codes and National Research Council of Canada, 2020), as implemented in the Global Earthquake Model (GEM) (2018). This model, which was used as the basis for the seismic hazard values in the 2020 National Building Code of Canada (2020 NBCC), consists of three regional models: the Western Model, the East Arctic Model, and the Southeastern Model. The Crawford Project site falls within the Southeastern Model.

The ground motion intensity for the Crawford Project site (Chapter 0) in Southeastern Canada is modeled using two sets of Ground Motion Models (GMMs) within the CanadaSHM6 framework. Each set is assigned an equal probability of 0.5. The first set, developed by Atkinson and Adams (2013)(AA13), includes three models, named "upper," "central," and "lower", to capture epistemic uncertainty. The central model, which represents the median ground motion, carries the highest weight. The second set of GMMs is derived from the Central and Eastern North America project (NGA-East-13) (Goulet, et al., 2017) and includes 13 candidate models, with weights that vary depending on the natural vibration period.

The seismic hazard assessment for the Crawford Project site was conducted using a Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Analysis (PSHA). A Deterministic Seismic Hazard Analysis (DSHA) is not necessary, as the site is located in a stable continental region with no known major active fault systems capable of producing large earthquakes. Consequently, identifying the Maximum Credible Earthquake through the DSHA approach, which depends on known faults, is less relevant for this location.

The PSHA for the Site was conducted using the OpenQuake v3.19.1 engine. Results of the PSHA are presented in terms of Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) and Uniform Hazard Spectra (UHS) for site conditions ranging from hard to soft rock, as defined by the 2020 NBCC (Chapter 6). The analysis considers events associated with a target AEP of 1:475, 1: 975, 1:2,475, 1:5,000 and 1:10,000 years and for various confidence levels, including mean, 50th, 84th, 90th, and 95th percentiles.

Dynamic site response analysis was used to modify the response spectra to the specific geotechnical conditions of each project facility (Chapter 6.5). This analysis involves estimating multi-period amplification factors dependent on the average shear-wave velocity of the upper 30 m of soil () as defined by the 2020 NBCC. Amplification factors were adopted from the from GMMs of the CanadaSHM6. Seismic Cone Penetration Tests (SCPT) conducted during the 2021-2022 and 2023 field investigations (SRK Consulting (Canada), Inc., 2023) (2024) provided  values ranging from 180 to 230 m/s. A characteristic value of 220 m/s was adopted for the site, classifying it as Stiff Soil Class D per the 2020 NBCC. The amplification factors were then applied to adjust the UHS for these site-specific conditions and were presented for target AEPs of ranging from 1:475 to 1:10,000 years and for various confidence levels.

The 2020 NBCC offers an online seismic hazard tool that provides seismic hazard values for building design across Canada (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021d). A comparison of the mean response spectra from this tool with the PSHA analysis was conducted, covering the relevant AEPs and structural periods (Chapter 8). The results demonstrate that the PSHA analysis aligns with the seismic hazard estimations used in the 2020 NBCC tool.

The Canadian Dam Association (CDA) (2013) along with the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) (2020) and the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) (2011), recommends performing PSHA and determining recurrence intervals based on the potential consequences of dam failure, which range from “Low” to “Extreme.” For this project, an “Extreme” consequence level has been designated for the FEED phase of the TMF, leading to a designation of the “Maximum Design Earthquake” (MDE) with an AEP of 1:10,000 years, consistent with GISTM and, for closure, with ICOLD and ANCOLD guidance. For the Clay, Rock, and Sand & Silt Impoundments, as well as the East and West Stockpiles, the MDE corresponds to an AEP of 1: 2,475 years. Response spectra and PGA values for the MDE have been provided for various site conditions, from hard rock to stiff soil, and at different confidence levels (Chapter 0). For stiff soils (220 m/s), the MDE for the TMF is anticipated to result in a horizontal Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) of 0.395 g (mean) and 0.491 g (84th percentile) and the MDE for the impoundments and stockpiles is anticipated to result in a PGA of 0.157 g (mean) and 0.198 g (84th percentile).

Seismic coefficients for the Crawford project embankments were estimated using an empirical (Bray, Macedo, & Travasauro, Simplified procedure for estimating seismic slope displacements for subduction and crustal earthquakes, 2018) (Chapter 0). The fundamental periods of the slopes were determined based on embankment configuration parameters, material types, and shear wave velocity values. The horizontal seismic coefficients were expressed as a percentage of the PGA for the MDE with an AEP of 1:10,000 years and were presented for various site conditions, including hard rock, soft rock, and stiff soil, and for different confidence levels. These coefficients, when applied to slope stability analyses, will provide estimates of the potential for failure during an MDE earthquake level.

Scope of Work

The scope of work, as defined in the proposal presented on June 7, 2024, between CNC and SRK-PC, includes the development of a Site-Specific Hazard Assessment for the Crawford Project, characterization the dynamic response of the slopes on specific dams and stockpiles, and preparation of a technical report. This work typically involves the assessment of the following aspects of this project:
Review of project background and seismotectonic framework, geotechnics, and historical seismicity. Update of the seismic catalog representing seismicity at the Site.
Identify and characterize seismogenic sources capable of generating significant ground motions within a 400-km radius of the project site. Select an appropriate source model.
Select a suite of ground motion prediction equations (GMPEs) and develop a logic tree framework that address epistemic uncertainty.

Conduct a full probabilistic seismic hazard assessment (PSHA) for the site, estimating annual exceedance probability (AEP) of ground accelerations for rock site conditions, Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA), and Uniform Hazard Spectra (UHS).

Estimate the site response for specific geotechnical conditions at the Site using an empirical method. Determine site classification in accordance to the 2020 National Building Code of Canada (Canadian Comission on Building and Fires Codes and National Research Council of Canada, 2020) and using available geotechnical data.

Define maximum design earthquakes (MDE) in accordance with guidelines from the Canadian Dam Association CDA (2013), Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management GISTM (International Council on Mining & Metals (ICMM), 2020), ICOLD, ANCOLD, and Seismic Hazard Criteria from the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) (2011).
Define horizontal seismic coefficients for the MDE, for a range of acceptable permanent deformations in the project embankments.
Prepare a comprehensive technical report summarizing the relevant results from the seismic hazard assessment.

Seismotectonics

Seismotectonics refers to the relationship between earthquake epicentral locations and active tectonic processes. In any given region, this relationship is governed by the relative motions of the Earth's lithospheric plates, which include both crustal and oceanic plates. These crustal plates can be further divided into older, more stable cratons and younger, less stable mobile belts. The interactions and relative movements of these plates generate regional stress fields, which are the primary drivers of tectonic earthquakes.
The main objective of this section is to outline the seismotectonic framework of the Site, providing insight into which sources may be seismically active.

The Site is located in the Northern Ontario region (NON in Figure 21), which extends from the Great Lakes to Hudson Bay. The physiography of Northern Ontario exemplifies a recently deglaciated shield terrain, characterized by numerous lakes, large exposures of crystalline bedrock, and glacial till deposits of variable thickness (Ma, Eaton, & Adams, 2008).

Although Northern Ontario earthquake activity rate is low as is part of the stable continental region, large and damaging earthquakes have occurred. The causes of earthquakes in this region have been primarily linked to:

Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA): ongoing process of the Earth's crust to rebound from the weight of the last ice sheets tat has been associated with seismicity in Northern Ontario (Ma, Eaton, & Adams, 2008) (Mazzotti, 2005) (Wu & Hasegawa, 1996), and crustal faults and fractures (Adams & Basham, 1991).

Regional intraplate stress: intraplate stress caused by ongoing deformation of the plate, including residual effects of ancient tectonic processes and current tectonic forces that can induce earthquakes (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021a; Adams & Basham, 1991).
Crustal faults and fractures: Existing weaknesses in the crust can be reactivated by the stresses associated with GIA and intraplate tectonic forces, leading to seismic events (Adams & Basham, 1991).

The most significant historic earthquake in the study area was the 1935 Temiskamingue earthquake, which had a magnitude of Mw 6.2. Following this, the 1928 earthquake near Otter Rapids and the 2000 Kipawa earthquake, both with magnitudes of Mw 4.7, were the second and third largest events, respectively. The 1935 Mw 6.2 Temiskamingue Earthquake

On November 1, 1935, at 1:03 am local time, an earthquake occurred about 10 km east of Témiscaming, Québec, approximately 285 km southeast of the Site. The earthquake was felt as far west as Thunder Bay, Ontario (later known as Fort William), as far east as the Bay of Fundy, and as far south as Kentucky and Virginia (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021d).

In Témiscaming, Québec, around 80% of chimneys were damaged, indicating a Modified Mercalli intensity of VII. Cracks also appeared in brick walls, and minor rockfalls were observed in the epicentral area. The shake caused significant damage in nearby Mattawa and North Bay, where many chimneys were destroyed. Numerous aftershocks were felt in Témiscaming and Kipawa in the months that followed. The day after the earthquake, Tee Lake's water near the epicenter was discolored, likely due to the resuspension of gyttja (freshwater mud). Additionally, 300 km away near Parent, Québec, the earthquake triggered a 30-meter railroad embankment slide (Natural Resources of Canada, 2021d).

Seismic Source Model
Definitions

The earthquake sources capable of generating significant ground motion at the site are identified and characterized using source models. This characterization involves defining the source geometry and the probability distributions of potential rupture locations within each source. The source models are classified into the following four seismic source model types:
Background Area-Source Models: These models use broad geographic zones where earthquakes can occur anywhere with equal probability.

Regional Area-Source Models: These models account for the non-uniform spatial distribution of seismicity at a regional scale, using historical seismicity patterns to forecast future earthquake occurrences.
Seismotectonic Models: These models integrate regional source models with fault-source models to provide a more comprehensive understanding of seismic potential.

Smoothed Seismicity Models: These data-driven models assume that historical seismicity is a reliable predictor of future seismic hazards, combining short-term data from the instrumental catalog with long-term geological information from fault-source models.
Each model type contributes unique insights to probabilistic hazard assessments. Additional epistemic uncertainty is addressed during the model parameterization process.

Seismic Hazard Assessment

The probability of exceeding a certain level of seismic intensity  at a given location is known as the seismic hazard of the site and can be estimated from the contribution of intensities from the different active faults of interest in the region.

A deterministic seismic hazard assessment (DSHA) postulates the existence of a seismic scenario where the maximum rupture size and the location of possible hypocenters are assumed to be known, upon which a ground-motion hazard evaluation is based. The controlling scenario from all possible seismic scenarios defines the maximum credible earthquake (MCE) in terms of magnitude and source-to-site distances.

Due to the random nature associated with the location of earthquake hypocenters and the size of the rupture area associated with during a seismic event, the distance to the fault  and the magnitude M are random variables that express in a simplified way the temporal and spatial variability, respectively, of the seismic motion.

A probabilistic seismic hazard assessment (PSHA) quantifies the contributions of all sources for all possible magnitudes within the affected area. In the same way as a DSHA, the PSHA stages identify all earthquake sources capable of producing significant ground-motion at the site and captures the expected range of all possible ground-motions in the target region. The spatial variability is given by all possible locations of the hypocenters of future seismic events that may affect the site. Temporal variability, on the other hand, is associated with the number of events per unit time that we should expect in each region and can be linked to the seismic magnitude and rupture area through the Guttenberg-Richter (1944) probability model.

The fundamental difference between PSHA and DSHA methodologies, is the inclusion of random uncertainty in the calculation of the spatial and temporal distribution of earthquakes, as well as the (aleatory) uncertainty associated with the ground-motion models.

DSHA analyses are not needed in geologically stable regions where major active fault systems capable of producing large earthquakes are absent. With no known active faults, the likelihood of a significant earthquake is low. In such areas, the deterministic approach, which relies on identifying the maximum credible earthquake from known faults, becomes less relevant.

Conclusions

SRK Consulting (Canada), Inc. (SRK) and Paterson and Cooke (P&C), collectively referred to as SRK-PC, were engaged by Canada Nickel Co. (CN) to perform a site-specific seismic hazard assessment for the Crawford Project near Timmins, Ontario. This assessment is part of the Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) for the proposed facilities. The key outcomes of the seismic hazard analysis are summarized below:
Seismic Hazard Assessment: A Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Analysis (PSHA) was conducted, providing essential design parameters such as peak ground acceleration (PGA) and spectral accelerations .

Seismicity of the Region: Although Northern Ontario is generally considered to be a region of low seismicity, the region experiences intraplate seismicity primarily driven by Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) and regional stress. Notable historical events, including the 1935 Temiskamingue earthquake (Mw 6.2) and the 2000 Kipawa earthquake (Mw 4.7), demonstrate the potential for earthquake activity.

Seismic Hazard Model: The assessment utilized the 6th Generation Seismic Hazard Model of Canada (CanadaSHM6), implemented through the Global Earthquake Model (GEM) (2018). This model forms the basis for seismic hazard values in the 2020 National Building Code of Canada (2020 NBCC) (Natural Resources of Canada, 2020).

Ground Motion Models: Two sets of Ground Motion Models (GMMs) were employed, capturing epistemic uncertainty. The models, developed by Atkinson and Adams (2013) and the NGA-East project (Goulet, et al., 2017) were used to model the ground motion intensity for the site.

PSHA: The PSHA for the site was conducted using the OpenQuake v3.19.1 engine (Pagani, Monelli, & Weatgerill, 2014). Results are presented in terms of Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) and Uniform Hazard Spectra (UHS) for site conditions ranging from hard to soft rock, as defined by the 2020 NBCC. The analysis considers events with target AEPs of 1:475, 1:975, 1:2,475, 1:5,000, and 1:10,000 years, and covers various confidence levels, including mean, 50th, 84th, 90th, and 95th percentiles.

Site-Specific Adjustments: Amplification factors were applied to the Uniform Hazard Spectra (UHS) to account for the site's geotechnical conditions. Seismic Cone Penetration Tests (SCPT) classified the site as Stiff Soil Class D (220 m/s) per the 2020 NBCC.

Design Earthquake (MDE): Based on GISTM, and for closure on ICOLD and ANCOLD guidance, an "Extreme" consequence level was adopted for the TMF, resulting in a Maximum Design Earthquake (MDE) with an AEP of 1:10,000 years. For Site Class D soils, the MDE corresponds to a horizontal PGA of 0.395 g (mean) and 0.491 g (84th percentile). For the Clay, Rock, and Sand & Silt Impoundments, as well as the East and West Stockpiles, the MDE corresponds to an AEP of 1:2,475 years, with a PGA of 0.157 g (mean) and 0.198 (84th percentile).

Seismic Coefficients: Performance-based seismic coefficients for embankments were derived from Newmark permanent displacements for use in pseudo-static slope stability analyses. The coefficients are reported at four relative displacement limits (0.1, 0.4, 1.0, and 2.5% of the slope height) for design earthquakes with AEPs of 1:475, 1:2,475, and 1:10,000 years.
